newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Bulgaria's UDF clear favourites to win election.
newsitem.headline: Bulgaria's UDF clear favourites to win election.

text.p: Compared to the euphoria of January and February's mass street protests, the campaign for Bulgaria's April 19 general election is a low-key affair.

The Union of Democratic Forces (UDF) are relying on the momentum of their campaign against the former Socialist government to propel them to victory, while the Socialists see little hope of reversing their fortunes in so short a time and are keeping their campaign low-key.
An opinion poll by Gallup published at the weekend showed support for the UDF at between 56 and 60 percent, with the Socialists and two smaller coalitions improving their share.

Socialist leader Georgi Parvanov said he felt his opponents were not trying hard enough. "They are relying too much on the benediction they got from the population during the January events," he told Reuters.
"If they carry on like this there is a possibility that they will quickly use up the credit they got from the people at the beginning of the year."

Campaigning is made more difficult because on the main issue, the economy, all parties have pledged their support for a tough reform programme agreed with the International Monetary Fund, leaving little room for manoeuvre.
The IMF board on Friday approved a $657 million package made up of a standby credit and a loan to buy grain.

The Socialists, ousted in February after 30 days of mass protests fuelled by economic hardship, oppose Bulgaria's application to join NATO, and accuse the UDF of wanting both to restore the monarchy and increase the president's powers.

The UDF, which was in opposition in the former parliament and can therefore blame all the country's ills on the ex-communist Socialists, says it is far too early even to think of such matters and the main priority is to fix the economy.

UDF leader Ivan Kostov said the new agreements with the IMF and other donors would improve financial discipline. "The strict compliance will deal a blow against corruption, racketeering and unfair competition," he said. "It will stop the chasing away of honest foreign and Bulgarian investors,"

But while the interim cabinet has dealt with the most acute phase of the crisis, UDF campaign pledges of security and prosperity sit ill with the IMF-prescribed target of cutting the budget deficit to 3.8 percent of GDP this year from last year's 12 percent.
The National Statistics Institute expects unemployment to rise from 13.7 percent in February to 17.7 percent by year end.
Much of the balance of payments support from the IMF, the European Union and other sources will go straight back to lenders as payments on Bulgaria's $9.65 billion foreign debt.
"I was surprised to hear our opponents promising everything to everyone when our agreement with the IMF makes such promises impossible," Parvanov said.

A glance at the televised debates shows that most of the hard work is being done by three smaller parties and coalitions with a chance of polling more than the four percent barrier for entering parliament.

The Alliance for National Salvation, a coalition including the ethnic Turkish Movement for Rights and Freedoms and several monarchist parties, has support of six to seven percent and could hold the balance of power in the new parliament.

Coalition leaders made a high-profile visit to exiled King Simeon in Madrid last week, though the king's spokeswoman in Sofia says he is the king of all Bulgarians and does not support any one party over another.

The Gallup poll gives the Euro-Left, a new coalition of leftist parties and Socialist defectors, four to six percent, while the Bulgarian Business Bloc, which in November's presidential election styled itself as the third force in Bulgarian politics, trails with 3.5 to 5.5 percent.

The Socialists livened up the campaign on Friday, claiming there had been a plan to stage a coup against their government last October by senior officers including the current interior ministry secretary, General Lyutskan Lyutskanov.
Commentators were sceptical about the announcement and its timing. "Pre-election truths are not true", read an editorial in Continent daily.
